The rhetorical situation: author, audience, purpose, context, message, medium
The three appeals — ethos (credibility/character), pathos (emotion), logos (logic/reasoning) — as analytic vocabulary, not a formula

The difference between analyzing rhetoric and judging it

claims.claim: Rhetorical analysis examines how a text persuades: it identifies the strategies a writer or speaker uses and explains how they work, rather than agreeing with the text or judging it first.

The rhetorical situation is the set of circumstances of a communication — the author (originator), the audience, the purpose, the context, the message, and the medium through which the message travels.
Ethos is the appeal based on the perceived character, credibility, or reliability of the writer or speaker; it persuades by building audience trust.
Pathos is the appeal to an audience's emotions, needs, and values, often carried by vivid language, personal stories, or sensory detail.
Logos is the appeal to reason through facts, examples, statistics, and clear reasoning; its force depends on the quality and relevance of the evidence presented.

Writers persuade through identifiable strategies such as repetition, parallel structure, word choice and connotation, anecdote, counterargument (acknowledging the opposition), rhetorical questions, and shifts in the text's projected attitude; analysis names the strategy and explains its effect on the audience.

Analyzing rhetoric and evaluating it are different moves: analysis describes how persuasion works in a text, while evaluation applies standards to judge whether the persuasion is effective, honest, or fair.
A rhetorical analysis is structured around a claim about a strategy, specific evidence from the text, and an explanation of the effect that strategy has on the intended audience.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Popular usage often treats 'rhetoric' as empty or deceptive speech, while academic usage treats it as the study of how language persuades.
positions: Rhetoric as trickery or spin (the dismissive everyday sense)
Rhetoric as the craft of persuasion (Aristotle: the available means of persuasion; Purdue OWL: any communication used to modify the perspectives of others)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines rhetoric as the craft or study of how language persuades, and notes that the same tools can be used ethically or deceptively; analysis describes the tools before any ethical judgment is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Ethos is sometimes equated narrowly with 'ethics' (moral rightness) and sometimes with the speaker's projected character or credibility.
positions: Ethos as strictly a moral appeal
Ethos as the appeal based on the perceived character, credibility, and reliability of the speaker (Purdue OWL; OpenStax)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the broader academic definition: ethos is the appeal to the speaker's perceived character, credibility, and trustworthiness, not a synonym for moralizing.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate (e.g., 'Rhetorical Analysis is a foundational concept in English & Literature') was discarded as machine-generated filler with no evidentiary basis.

The draft's statement that rhetorical analysis 'is used as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' is generic and unsupported as stated; the lesson replaces it with specific, sourced claims about analyzing persuasion.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic generated draft entirely with a source-verified lesson.
Presented the appeals as an analytic vocabulary rather than a fixed three-part formula, per OpenStax 9.1/9.3, which describe appeals and strategies as building blocks writers combine.
Clarified the analysis-versus-evaluation distinction, which the draft did not address.
Added the claim-evidence-effect paragraph structure for writing a rhetorical analysis, grounded in OpenStax 9.5.

sourceRecords.title: 1.1 "Reading" to Understand and Respond (Rhetoric and the Rhetorical Situation)
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the official OpenStax Writing Guide PDF (assets.openstax.org/oscms-prodcms/media/documents/WritingGuide-WEB.pdf), section 1.1; the canonical URL was verified live (HTTP 200). Supports the rhetorical situation as agents (originator and audience, real or anticipated) and conditions (genre/medium, purpose, stance, context, culture), and the definition of reading rhetorically as figuring out why and how a message works. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 9.1 Breaking the Whole into Its Parts
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the official OpenStax Writing Guide PDF, section 9.1; the canonical URL was verified live (HTTP 200). Supports: Aristotle's definition of rhetoric as the means of persuasion in speaking and writing; ethos as a believable, authoritative voice that elicits trust; pathos as appeals to shared feelings and emotions; logos as credible information (facts, reasons, examples) moving toward a sensible conclusion; kairos as timeliness; and the statement that the aim of rhetorical analysis is not agreement or praise but identifying the writer's tools and what they accomplish. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 9.3 Glance at Genre: Rhetorical Strategies
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the official OpenStax Writing Guide PDF, section 9.3; the canonical URL was verified live (HTTP 200). Supports: the strategy list (establishing credibility, sharing personal experience, targeting emotional concerns, using devices such as parallelism, repetition, and rhetorical questions to draw attention to claims, supporting claims with quotations, anecdotes, examples, statistics, and acknowledging the opposition); definitions of repetition, parallel structure, rhetorical question, and figurative language with examples; and the 'aim of rhetorical analysis is not to find agreement with or praise for the writer' detachment principle. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 9.5 Writing Process: Thinking Critically about Rhetoric
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the official OpenStax Writing Guide PDF, section 9.5; the canonical URL was verified live (HTTP 200). Supports how to structure a rhetorical analysis: decide which statements are most effective, organize paragraph by paragraph or strategy by strategy, open each body paragraph with a topic sentence stating a point of analysis, provide quotations, explain how the strategy functions and supports or fails to support the writer's position, address ethos/pathos/logos and counterclaims, and use the conclusion to confirm an evaluation of effectiveness. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.
